The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.

Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. content.text:
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 4
PROPOSITION 1
Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative
Statute.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and
apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private
dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the
case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments,
nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of
the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or
rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership
Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various
housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a
development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general
obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to
provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges
who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home
loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan.
Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to
provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds
through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for
veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 4
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell
$11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a
$10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General
Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home
loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including
education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported
bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing
programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of
years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
• Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to
acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings. These
programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-
interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must
reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this
funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site services (such
as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
• Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support
homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would
be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans
that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other
funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities
such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and
repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
• Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of
infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water,
sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
• Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and
grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for
both rental and owner-occupied housing.
• Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million,
split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for
affordable student housing.
• Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes.
Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and
repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
• Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to
cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing
housing at reduced costs.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 4
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan
assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences,
condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state
General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about
25 years. The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of
the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows,
the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if
the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home
loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds.
These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has
always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to
administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other
government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for
up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about
1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including
about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting
the production and repair of homes.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 4 of 4
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support
veterans and affordable housing.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support
veterans and affordable housing.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay
the housing bond.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25
years to repay the housing bond.

Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. There’s a $11.25 billion housing bond on the ballot this November. Here’s what you should know

By Marisa Kendall, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 aims to address that crisis.

It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. 

A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes.

Legislators have passed multiple laws trying to address that by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. 

A recent report estimated nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them.

What would Prop. 1 do?

Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative
Statute.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and
apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private
dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the
case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments,
nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of
the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or
rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership
Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various
housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a
development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general
obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to
provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges
who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home
loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan.
Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to
provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds
through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for
veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 4
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell
$11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a
$10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General
Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home
loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including
education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported
bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing
programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of
years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
• Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to
acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings. These
programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-
interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must
reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this
funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site services (such
as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
• Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support
homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would
be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans
that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other
funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities
such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and
repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
• Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of
infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water,
sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
• Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and
grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for
both rental and owner-occupied housing.
• Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million,
split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for
affordable student housing.
• Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes.
Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and
repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
• Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to
cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing
housing at reduced costs.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 4
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan
assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences,
condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state
General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about
25 years. The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of
the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows,
the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if
the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home
loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds.
These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has
always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to
administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other
government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for
up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about
1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including
about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting
the production and repair of homes.

A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 4
PROPOSITION 1
Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative
Statute.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and
apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private
dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the
case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments,
nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of
the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or
rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership
Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various
housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a
development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general
obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to
provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges
who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home
loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan.
Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to
provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds
through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for
veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 2 of 4
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell
$11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a
$10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General
Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home
loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including
education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported
bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing
programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of
years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
• Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to
acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings. These
programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-
interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must
reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this
funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site services (such
as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
• Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support
homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would
be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans
that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other
funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities
such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and
repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
• Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of
infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water,
sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
• Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and
grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for
both rental and owner-occupied housing.
• Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million,
split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for
affordable student housing.
• Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes.
Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and
repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
• Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to
cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing
housing at reduced costs.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 3 of 4
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan
assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences,
condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state
General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about
25 years. The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of
the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows,
the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if
the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home
loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds.
These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has
always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to
administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other
government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for
up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about
1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including
about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting
the production and repair of homes.
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 4 of 4
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support
veterans and affordable housing.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support
veterans and affordable housing.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay
the housing bond.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25
years to repay the housing bond.

For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Sign up for free Δ Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.

So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.

That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.
This is a fundamental problem with California’s focus on 100% affordable housing developments — rents don’t cover the bills, necessitating significant ongoing subsidies.

Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.
Wicks told us California also needs to restructure its budgets to establish “sustained ongoing funding for affordable housing so that we’re not having to have this bond conversation every six years.”

Is the answer to California’s housing crisis more bonds and more debt? Of course not.
Yet that’s what’s being pitched with Proposition 1.
Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature via Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), Prop. 1 asks voters to approve (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) $11.25 billion in bonds to help finance various programs, including a $500 million down payment assistance program.
One bond – $1.25 billion – will go toward the Department of Veteran Affairs (CalVet) Home Loan Program. Participants in the program will repay this portion of Prop. 1.
The other $10 billion bond will be paid out of the state’s General Fund, and will go toward various programs. Most of it will go toward subsidized housing for low-income residents, while other funds will go toward programs aimed at student housing, tribes and farmworkers.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, Prop. 1 “would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students.”
Proponents say Prop. 1 is worth the cost given the state’s high rate of homelessness and the high proportion of renters who struggle with high housing costs. In backing the measure, California YIMBY argues that, “Publicly-funded housing subsidies for low-income Californians who cannot afford market-rate rents are a good thing, and they should be more widely available.”
Yeah, no.
Taxpayer-subsidized housing in California is incredibly expensive to build. As a RAND Corp. report (https://backtobasicssj.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/RAND_RRA3743-1.pdf) from last year points out, publicly-subsidized “affordable” housing in California costs 1.5 times that of market rate housing “and more than four times the cost of market-rate housing in Texas.”
There are myriad reasons for this, of course. As much progress as California has made in loosening zoning laws, the state’s land-use policies remain restrictive. Permitting processes in major cities are often incredibly slow (https://x.com/esoltas/status/2098162675989565925/photo/1) . Reprieves from the California Environmental Quality Act always come with costly strings attached, including labor mandates.
Throwing more money into housing that’s slow and expensive to build simply won’t accomplish very much, because it can’t.
California YIMBY, to its credit, also points out some of the less desirable features of the measure. The down payment assistance program, for example, might be nice for those who benefit from it, but given the low supply of housing, it could end up contributing to higher home prices.
Then there’s the total bill for all of this. The $10 billion general obligation bond will, after interest, cost far more than that and further crowd-out other spending in the state budget. According to the LAO, the state will be spending $500 million to $600 million a year for 25 years to pay off the bond.
This, in turn, will only put further pressure on the perpetually precarious state budget and increase the risk of the Legislature approving or seeking new and higher taxes. This is no idle threat considering state lawmakers contemplated hundreds of billions of dollars (https://www.caltax.org/foundation/reports/20260611_Tax_and_Fee_Report.pdf) in new taxes this legislative session.
Eight years ago, in opposing the very similar Proposition 1 in 2018, we wrote (https://www.dailybreeze.com/2018/09/18/proposition-1-is-not-the-answer-to-our-housing-crisis-vote-no/) , “If California’s leaders are serious about making California a more affordable place to live, they should concentrate their efforts on curtailing onerous regulations and restrictive land-use policies and making it easier for homebuilders to build. And if they insist on subsidizing housing, they should do so directly, rather than wasting taxpayer money on interest payments.”
We stand by that, though we’d emphasize the need for California to stop fiddling and burdening reforms with mandates. There are those who argue California can both subsidize housing and loosen regulations, but the reality that we’re still having this discussion underscores that state and local leaders are dragging their feet and not deregulating fast enough.
California needs more housing, yes, but it doesn’t need Prop. 1.
Prop. 1 squanders billions into expensive housing and other gimmicks to buy political support.
Vote no and demand better housing policies.

# Key findings
A subsidized apartment built with California tax credits cost about $630,000 per unit in 2023, up nearly 20% since 2019 after inflation. [1]
The state's share in this bond works out to roughly $180,000 per rental unit ($7.2B for up to 40,000 units, our math). The rest has to come from tax credits and local money. [2]
RAND estimates that at Colorado's cost levels, about $1.25B of recent spending by California's four biggest housing programs would have built more than 4 times as many units . [3]
The State Auditor has flagged the agency that runs these bonds (HCD) in five audits (2007–2018) : weak monitoring, unexplained high per-unit costs, and a data system that never worked fully. [4] [5] [6]
The campaign is funded mostly by the groups that would apply for the money: $13.9M of $15.3M came from a committee sponsored by affordable-housing organizations. [7]
The split you vote on isn't fixed. The bond act lets the Legislature "amend this chapter in order to reallocate the proceeds" among its programs by ordinary statute, with no further vote of the people. [8]

# Money and conflicts
Yes $15.3M, No $0 in committees (through Oct 22). [7] Reform California has spent about $7,500 against. [12] Top Yes donors include Airbnb, two carpenters' union councils, and Building a Better California (funded by Sergey Brin and John Doerr), at $1M each. [14]
Recipients are mostly nonprofit and for-profit affordable-housing developers, who apply to HCD and CalHFA. For example, MidPen Housing alone has 1,198 units waiting on state money. [15]
Supporters cite 461 "shovel-ready" projects (39,880 units) stalled for lack of gap funding. That count comes from Enterprise Community Partners, an affordable-housing finance group. [15]
# Does it solve a lasting problem?
It adds units, but it doesn't touch the cost per unit, which is the main reason each dollar builds so little. Every extra funding source a project needs adds about 4 months and ~$20,460 per unit. [1] [15]
The state needs about 1 million lower-income units by 2030 under its own targets. This bond covers roughly 4% of that. [15] [2]
Our read is a toss-up. The backlog of ready projects is real and no one is organized against the bond. But the evidence on this page runs one way: cost per unit is the problem, the bond doesn't touch it, the agency has left the 2018 audit fixes untouched, and the campaign is funded by the applicants. Vote yes if you weigh the backlog more; vote no if you want the cost problem fixed first.
# If you vote yes: accountability
Bottom line: Most of the $10B goes out as competitive awards from one department (HCD) with no cost-per-unit limit in the law. The bill only requires an annual report (§ 54088), and it lets agencies write the program rules without the usual public rulemaking (§ 54077). [8] Watching how the money is spent is up to voters, reporters and the Legislature.

# Who gets the money
Applicants are nonprofit and for-profit developers, cities, counties and tribes. From 2019 to 2025, HCD funded 66,511 rental units . Of those, 26,904 (40%) are listed as completed so far , and 14,660 hadn't started construction. Projects funded in the last two or three years can't be finished yet, so the number to watch is whether the older awards close out. [21]
No single public database lists each HCD award with its developer, cost per unit and status. HCD's summary gives counts only. The best project-level records are CTCAC's staff reports, which list each tax-credit project's developer, units and total cost. [22]
# Red flags already on record
Fraud charges: Shangri-La Industries won about $115M in state Homekey contracts for about 500 homes. Its $27M Thousand Oaks project sits abandoned. Its former CFO was federally charged with mail fraud in Oct 2025 and has pleaded not guilty. [23] [17] The state, through Attorney General Bonta, sued the company in Jan 2024, alleging breach of contract and fraud. [24]
Close to home: San Bernardino's All Star Lodge, a Homekey motel conversion, was foreclosed after two years. No affordability restriction had been recorded, so the new owner could threaten big rent increases. [17] [25]
Homekey's record: $3.8B awarded since 2020. About 1 in 5 promised homes were unfinished at the end of 2024, and at least 10 awards (about 500 units) were canceled or clawed back. No state agency has publicly analyzed the program in detail. [17] This matters here because Prop 1's $1.15B supportive-housing share can fund the same kind of interim-to-permanent conversions. [8]
Audit advice ignored: In 2018 the State Auditor told the Legislature to require HCD to report every year on how it monitors bond programs, and to have its parent agency track HCD's progress. As of Jan 2026, the status of both is "No action taken." The audit's recommendations on HCD's administrative-cost overspending are still listed as only partially implemented or pending. [6]
Money lost, units unclear: A state committee let about $2.7B in housing bond authority expire in 2015–2017 without saying so publicly. The housing agencies don't share a project ID, so their unit counts may overlap. [26]
Evaluation blocked: AB 505 would have had the LAO evaluate Homekey. It died in the Assembly Housing Committee in Jan 2026 without a hearing. [27]
Not on the high-risk list: The State Auditor's Dec 2025 high-risk list doesn't include housing or homelessness spending. [28]
# Who to press, and what to ask for
Your Assemblymember and state Senator (look them up at findyourrep.legislature.ca.gov). Ask them to:
Pass the 2018 audit recommendation into law: public, project-by-project reporting for every Prop 1 award (developer, units, cost per unit, start and completion dates).
Ask the Joint Legislative Audit Committee to have the State Auditor audit the first round of Prop 1 awards. Any legislator can request an audit.
Bring back the Homekey evaluation that AB 505 proposed.
Lower the cost per unit: fund each project from fewer sources, since each extra source adds about 4 months and $20,460 per unit [1] [15] , and adopt RAND's recommendations: a 30-day approval deadline, synchronized inspections, lower impact fees ($29,000 per unit in California vs. $12,000 in Colorado), and fewer design rules that don't affect safety. [3]
Treasurer and Controller candidates: they'll sit on CTCAC. Ask whether they'll score tax-credit applications on cost per unit and publish final costs for every finished project.
CTCAC and HCD meetings take public comment. Agendas are posted on the Treasurer's and HCD's websites.
Report waste or fraud to the State Auditor's whistleblower hotline: auditor.ca.gov/hotline or 800-952-5665. You can file anonymously. [29]
# Public records to request (CPRA)
The California Public Records Act is the state's version of FOIA. Anyone can file a request, and you don't need to give a reason. The agency must respond within 10 days, or within 24 days in unusual cases. [30] Send HCD requests through its online portal or to PRARequest@hcd.ca.gov (mailto:PRARequest@hcd.ca.gov). [31]
To HCD: Under the California Public Records Act (Gov. Code § 7920.000 et seq.), I request records sufficient to show, for every award made from Proposition 1 (2018) and Proposition 1 (2024) bond funds: project name, sponsor and developer, city, award amount and date, number of units, total development cost, and current status (not started, under construction, or completed, with the completion date). I also request any notices of default, recapture or cancellation for these awards. I prefer electronic records in their original format, such as a spreadsheet. Please state the estimated date the records will be available, as Gov. Code § 7922.535 requires.
To HCD: All monitoring reports, notices of default, and recapture or settlement records for Homekey projects sponsored by Shangri-La Industries, and for the All Star Lodge in San Bernardino.
To CTCAC (State Treasurer's Office): For every tax-credit project in San Bernardino County awarded from 2019 to 2025, the final cost certification showing the total development cost at completion, alongside the cost in the application.
What it does
$10B of the general-obligation bonds, repaid from the General Fund: $7.2B affordable rentals, $1.1B homeownership, $500M infrastructure, $450M farmworker housing, $350M UC/CSU student housing, $200M tribal housing, $200M local pilots. [2]
$1.25B CalVet home loans, repaid by veterans' loan payments (the program "has always operated at no direct cost to the state"). [2]
Cost: $500–600M a year for about 25 years. [2]
What we're not asking
Each bond is bigger and buys less. State housing bonds went $2.1B (2002), $2.85B (2006), $4B (2018), $11.25B (2026), while the cost of a tax-credit unit rose nearly 20% after inflation from 2019 to 2023. [9] [2] [1] Play it forward: a yes vote with no cost reform sets up a larger ask around 2030.
Subsidy chases a fixed pipeline. Most of these projects also need federal tax credits, which are capped. More state gap money doesn't add credits; it funds the same projects with one more layer, and each extra source adds about 4 months and $20,460 per unit. [1] [15]
The debt stacks. The state had $70.7B in general-obligation bonds outstanding and $39.9B authorized but unsold as of March 2026. Prop 1 adds $10B and Prop 38 another $8.4B, each costing $500–600M a year from the same General Fund that pays for schools and Medi-Cal. [16] [2]
Who checks year 30? Affordability covenants run for decades, but at the All Star Lodge in San Bernardino no covenant was even recorded. Nobody is funded to monitor covenants over the life of the bond. [17]
Game theory. Developers fund the campaign, win the awards, and fund the next bond. The Legislature can shift the split later by statute. HCD has no reason to fix its data when the money comes anyway. The bond vote is the only lever voters hold.
Better or worse in 20 years? Roughly 40,000 households housed, which is real. The cost structure, the data gap and the debt all stay. More units, same machine.
Open questions: Why does the bill cap nothing per unit? Where is the completed-unit count for the 2018 bond? Would a smaller bond tied to a cost cap have passed the Legislature?
Both sides
For: a real backlog of ready projects; rents are crushing low-income households; the bond funds farmworker, tribal and student housing that the market won't build.
Against: No official ballot argument against was filed. [32] Republican lawmakers, including Asm. Carl DeMaio, say only ~11% goes to veterans despite the name [12] , and that it borrows without addressing why building here costs so much [17] [33] ; RAND finds that at Colorado's costs, the same money would build 4x+ as many units. Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

Article continues below this ad
Endorsement : Who should replace Nancy Pelosi in Congress? It’s not even a choice (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/scott-wiener-connie-chan-pelosi-22448323.php)
Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.
